forces: Boy soprano solo, orchestra and organ
performers: Denis Thilliez, boy soprano; Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo, Louis Frémaux
question: How much can one line of text say when it is sung three times?
intro: A boy soprano sings one line of the Dies irae three times, over a solo organ stop, muted strings and a few winds. Listen for how the second call rises and how the third returns to the first.

sections.label: Second call, higher
sections.mNote: the call repeats, pitched higher and louder

sections.label: Third call, with winds
sections.mNote: the first melody returns with woodwind

sections.label: Sempiternam requiem · close
sections.mNote: the two-note plea in a lower range

cues.title: A boy soprano over organ
cues.text: A boy soprano sings “Pie Jesu Domine, dona eis requiem”, marked “dolce e tranquille”, over a solo organ stop. The strings, harp and winds rest in these first bars. The melody is modal and gentle, in B♭ major.
cues.evidence: Page 61 of the score gives the soprano solo line, the organ marked “Récit. Solo. 8 pieds” and rests in every other staff. The report’s level rises from −30.0 dB at 0:00 to −16.3 dB at 0:05, with onset density of 4.2 per second at 0:05 and B♭ major as the local key estimate (0.64 to 0.91) through 0:40. Wikipedia’s description calls the first call modal.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Only the last verse
cues.text: Pie Jesu is the final verse of the Dies irae sequence, and the only part of it Fauré set. Following a French Baroque custom, he omitted the rest, so a single quiet prayer stands where other Requiems set pages of judgement.
cues.evidence: The Text section of the Wikipedia article on the Requiem says Fauré followed a French Baroque tradition by not setting the Dies irae, only its section Pie Jesu.

cues.title: The second call, higher
cues.text: Around 0:50 the call returns higher and a little louder, marked “un poco più”. Before it, muted strings, harp and woodwind place soft chords under the voice; the organ keeps moving beneath the soprano.
cues.evidence: The report finds a cluster of boundaries at 0:44, 0:48, 0:52 and 0:56 (0.32 to 0.38), with level rising from −17.1 dB at 0:40 to −11.7 dB at 0:50. Pages 62–63 of the score show the pp chords in winds, harp and strings and the soprano restarting at letter A marked un poco più.

cues.title: Two notes, said twice
cues.text: From about 1:20 the soprano expands on “dona eis, Domine, dona eis requiem”, then alternates between just two notes on “sempiternam requiem”, twice. The strings and organ carry the motion while the voice stays almost still.
cues.evidence: The report’s strongest boundary is 1:24 (1.00), and the loudest windows of the first half are 1:20 (−10.4 dB), 1:25 (−9.9 dB) and 1:40 (−10.8 dB). Pages 65–66 of the score (letters B and C) give the expanded phrase and the repeated two-note “sempiternam requiem”.

cues.title: A boy’s voice
cues.text: The soloist is Denis Thilliez, a boy soprano of the Manécanterie des Petits Chanteurs Notre-Dame de Sainte-Croix de Neuilly. Fauré’s Madeleine admitted no women singers, though in concert he preferred women for this solo.
cues.evidence: The scanned Erato sleeve credits Denis Thilliez, “soprano garçon”, of the Manécanterie named above; it names no other soprano, and the Pie Jesu is the Requiem’s only soprano solo. The History and Versions sections of the Wikipedia article on the Requiem give the Madeleine’s rule and Fauré’s preference for female sopranos in the concert hall.

cues.title: The first melody returns
cues.text: Near 2:08 the opening melody comes back for the third and last call, now with solo woodwind marked “dolce” beside the soprano. The plea ends on alternating notes in a lower range, with a poco ritenuto and a gentle upward turn on the last “requiem”.
cues.evidence: The report finds boundaries at 2:08 (0.32) and 2:34 (0.31), with level rising from −19.7 dB at 2:00 to −9.8 dB at 2:10 and falling to −27.7 dB at 2:55. Pages 67–69 of the score (letters D and E) show the woodwind solos, poco rit. and the soprano’s final phrase; Wikipedia’s description gives the lower two-note plea and the upward turn.

cues.title: The sleeve writer, once a treble
cues.text: The liner note is signed by Louis Aubert, who recalls singing the Requiem’s solo soprano part at twelve, a few months after the 1888 first performance. Wikipedia names Aubert as the treble in the first performance itself.
cues.evidence: The scanned sleeve, signed Louis Aubert, says he was solo soprano of the Madeleine choir school at twelve, some months after the first performance. The History section of the Wikipedia article on the Requiem names Louis Aubert as the treble soloist on 16 January 1888; the two accounts differ in date.

transitions.title: A second, higher call
transitions.how: The first call ends and muted strings, harp and woodwind place soft chords beneath the organ, a change from the organ-and-voice texture of the first bars. At letter A the soprano begins again, marked “un poco più”, and the phrase reaches higher than before. The words and the melodic shape return; what changes is register, level and the amount of orchestral colour around the voice.
transitions.evidence: The report finds boundaries at 0:44, 0:48, 0:52 and 0:56 (0.32 to 0.38), with level rising from −17.1 dB at 0:40 to −11.7 dB at 0:50. Pages 62–63 of the score show the pp chords in winds, harp and strings and the restart at letter A; Wikipedia’s description says the second call is similar but reaches higher.

transitions.title: The plea turns to two notes
transitions.how: After the second call, letter B brings “dona eis, Domine, dona eis requiem”, which begins with more expansion than the earlier calls, then settles into two alternating notes on “sempiternam requiem”, repeated. Fauré reduces the melody to a pair of pitches while the strings and organ supply the motion beneath. The plea becomes simpler as it grows more urgent: the accompaniment swells beneath it, then ebbs.
transitions.evidence: The report’s strongest boundary is 1:24 (1.00); level rises from −14.9 dB at 1:15 to −10.4 dB at 1:20 and −9.9 dB at 1:25 and stays near −11 dB at 1:40. Pages 65–66 of the score give letters B and C, with poco cresc. markings in the strings and organ.

transitions.title: The first melody returns with winds
transitions.how: After the two-note “sempiternam requiem”, the opening melody returns at letter D as the third and last call, now with solo woodwind lines marked “dolce” beside the soprano. Fauré brings back the beginning rather than developing the plea further. What was first heard over a solo organ stop now sounds with flute, clarinet and bassoon around it, so the return is recognisable but warmer.
transitions.evidence: The report finds a boundary at 2:08 (0.32), with level rising from −19.7 dB at 2:00 to −13.9 dB at 2:05 and −9.8 dB at 2:10. Page 67 of the score marks letter D, the soprano’s “Pie Jesu” and the woodwind solos; Wikipedia’s description says the last call begins as the first.

transitions.title: The last plea sinks lower
transitions.how: The third call leads again to two alternating notes, now in an even lower range. At letter E the harp’s pianissimo figure continues beneath the soprano and the pace relaxes with a “poco rit.”. The final “requiem” has a gentle upward motion. The movement closes pianissimo, without a climax: the prayer’s last word is not a peak but the quietest point of the line.
transitions.evidence: The report finds a boundary at 2:34 (0.31), with level near −17 dB to 2:50 and falling to −27.7 dB at 2:55 and −51 dB at 3:00. Page 69 of the score (letter E) marks poco rit. and the pianissimo harp figure; Wikipedia’s description gives the lower alternating notes and the final upward motion.

source.title: Fauré, Requiem, Op. 48, full orchestral score (Hamelle, 1901; Kalmus reprint)
source.locator: IV. Pie Jesu, printed pp. 61–69. The viola, cello and bass parts are marked “Sourdines” (muted); the violin staff rests throughout. The chorus, trumpet, trombone and timpani staves are empty throughout. Entries are set from the page layout and the report’s boundaries, so an instrument that plays in only part of a span is listed for the whole span.

timeline.note: The boy soprano sings over a solo organ stop; the muted strings, harp and winds rest.
Muted strings, harp and woodwind add pianissimo chords beneath the soprano and organ.
The second call is sung over the organ alone.
Woodwind, harp and muted strings again add pianissimo figures before letter B.
The soprano’s “dona eis” and two-note plea are carried by muted strings and organ.
The opening melody returns with solo woodwind marked dolce beside the soprano.
The plea sinks to a lower two-note figure over a pianissimo harp, with a poco ritenuto at the end.
A first bassoon adds a solo line in the last two bars; flute and clarinet rest.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Denis Thilliez (boy soprano), Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo (orchestra), Louis Frémaux (conductor), Henri Carol (organ)
fields.note: Commons lists Bernard Kruysen and Denis Thilliez among the artists of the complete recording. The sleeve credits “Denis Thilliez, soprano garçon” as the only soprano soloist, and the Pie Jesu is the Requiem’s only soprano solo, so his part here is inferred rather than stated. The chorus and baritone have no part in this movement.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Full-orchestra version, as published by Éditions Hamelle (1901)
fields.note: The sleeve credits “Editions Hamelle – Paris” and describes the version heard as the one with the more extended symphonic forces, which it says Fauré transcribed around 1899; Hamelle published the full-orchestra score in 1901. The sleeve names no editor or corrections, and the forces were not checked by ear against the score. Wikipedia notes that the 1900 autograph does not survive and that critics have asked who scored it, so authorship of the orchestration is not asserted here. The orchestra panel uses the Kalmus reprint of the Hamelle score.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The scanned Erato sleeve prints “Enregistré … à Monaco, le 11 Août 1962”. The Commons date field (“10 August 1962”), IMSLP and René Gagnaux give 10 August 1962; Commons does not say whether its date is a session or an issue date. The 1988 CD reissue notes “Recording: 08/1962”. Both candidate days fall in 1962; the rights assessment relies on that year only.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco
fields.note: The sleeve gives the cathedral in Monaco, and a 1983 Erato LP pressing (EF 28002) is noted on Discogs as “Registered in 1962 in the Cathedral of Monaco”. IMSLP and Gagnaux give the Salle Alcazar, Monte-Carlo. Commons gives no venue. The sleeve also credits the engineer: “Prise de son : Peter Willemoes”.
alts: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Commons names “Erato Records” as source; the sleeve, BnF and Discogs give the Erato label.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The BnF notices list both issues with a 1962 legal-deposit date and cross-reference each other; the sleeve says the disc also exists in stereo as STE 50 128. Commons does not say which pressing, tape or CD its file derives from. The access MP3 is two-channel with a left/right correlation of 0.88 in this movement, so it is not a mono transfer, but that does not identify the carrier.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No matrix or take numbers appear in the sources consulted. The sleeve lays out this movement as face 1, track 4 of the LP (face 1: Introït et Kyrie, Offertoire, Sanctus, Pie Jesu; face 2: Agnus Dei, Libera me, In paradisum, then the Cantique de Jean Racine).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is identified. Commons shows the file as uploaded by D. Benjamin Miller; an uploader is not assumed to be the engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Commons upload date (23 May 2018) is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: No source-transfer or restoration processing is disclosed. Contrapunctus’ own analysis estimates the reference pitch of this movement about 40 to 60 cents above A = 440 Hz (+40 cents (CQT histogram) and +0.37 semitone (librosa estimate_tuning)); all seven movements of the set give a similar offset. Whether it comes from the orchestra’s tuning, the disc speed or the transfer speed is not established, and Hz and note names in the analysis report are not corrected for it.

fields.value: Public domain in jurisdictions applying an unextended life-plus-70-year term
fields.note: Gabriel Fauré died in 1924. This assessment concerns the original composition, not a later edition, arrangement or this recording; it is not a worldwide rights clearance.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial: sound recording in the public domain in the European Union (Commons PD-EU-audio; first published before 1963).
fields.note: Commons applies {{PD-EU-audio}} alone to this file (wikitext inspected at the cited revision; source “Erato Records”, date field 1962-08-10). The BnF catalogue records legal deposit in 1962 (“1962 (DL)”) for both Erato issues, LDE 3228 and STE 50128: that is the best primary evidence found that first publication came before 1963, so the 50-year EU term had expired before the term extension applied to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013 (Directive 2011/77/EU, Article 1(3)). Legal deposit is not an exact publication date and no issue month was found. The “℗ Erato Disques S.A. 1963” line on the 1988 CD reissue (ECD 40006) belongs to that reissue and is not taken as the date of first publication. A recording or session date is not used as a publication date. This is territorial and does not establish US sound-recording status.

composer.epithet: A church organist who made the French song and the chamber ensemble laboratories for harmony.
facts: École Niedermeyer, 1854–65; piano with Camille Saint-Saëns
Madeleine: choirmaster 1877–96, organist 1896–1905 · Paris Conservatoire: composition professor 1896–1905, director 1905–20
Mélodies, piano music, chamber music, Requiem, the opera Pénélope
composer.background:
Fauré learned his trade in a school for church musicians. His father was a schoolmaster in the Ariège; at nine, Gabriel was sent to Louis Niedermeyer’s recently founded school in Paris, where plainchant, Renaissance polyphony, organ playing and counterpoint belonged to the ordinary curriculum. The education matters to the harmony. A melody can cadence in minor with an unsharpened seventh degree; a chord can emerge from the independent movement of voices. These possibilities were practical knowledge before they became a recognisable Fauré style.

After Niedermeyer died in 1861, Camille Saint-Saëns took over the piano class and introduced the pupils to Schumann, Liszt and Wagner. Teacher and pupil remained friends for more than sixty years. Fauré’s graduation work, the Cantique de Jean Racine of 1865, already joins the two educations: a flowing keyboard accompaniment beneath a choral texture whose entries are controlled by contrapuntal discipline. Its French text is Racine’s paraphrase of a Latin hymn. The bass supports long phrases that carry the upper voices across the bar-lines.
